questions.help:
12 Distances
 
12.5 Safety distance
The safety distance is the minimum space that a driver should leave between their vehicle and the vehicle ahead of them. This should be sufficient and enable them to stop, without impacting and colliding with the vehicle ahead of them, in the case of hard or unexpected braking by the preceding vehicle (the vehicle ahead of them). For safety it should always be greater than the stopping distance of the vehicle.
Not respecting the safety distance from the vehicle in front of you is the main cause of rear-end crashes.
This distance should be increased when travelling at higher speeds or in reduced visibility, or where the road has low adhesion qualities and when the driver is unsure of the locality or lacks experience.
Not maintaining the safety distance with the vehicle driving ahead of you can cost 4 points.
 
(Página 180 del manual 'Learning to drive')

12 Distances
 
12.5 Safety distance
Any driver of a vehicle driving behind another must leave space that allows them to stop without colliding in the event of sudden braking, taking into account, in particular, speed, grip and braking conditions. However, a group of cyclists does not need to keep this distance, paying close attention to avoid collisions.
When it is possible for vehicles behind you to overtake, then in addition to leaving a sufficient separation distance so that in case of sudden braking by the vehicle ahead of you – you don’t crash into the back of it, you should additionally leave a gap to allow overtaking vehicles to overtake safely. (Note: that his rule is not applicable to a group of cyclists travelling together.)
Vehicles with a MAM greater than 3500 kgs, vehicles and combinations / sets of vehicles over 10m long, must keep a minimum safety distance of 50 m.
(Página 180 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
Safe driving      
     
5 Driving in rain
5.1.1 Aquaplaning
Aquaplaning (also referred to occasionally as ‘hydroplaning’) is a frightening phenomenon whereby a wedge (or film) of water builds up between the tyres and the road surface. The depth of water on the road may be excessive for the grooves of the tyre to suitably displace it, which may also be heightened because of an inadequate depth of tyre tread.  
This causes the vehicle to feel like it is “gliding or sliding on the water”. The result is complete loss of normal control by the driver.
(Página 228 del manual 'Learning to drive')

Safe driving      
       
5 Driving in rain
5.1.1 Aquaplaning
Aquaplaning is caused by the accumulation of water on the road and by irregularities in its surface. Therefore, when it rains, it is necessary to pay special attention to potholes and areas in which puddles may occur.
This effect is more likely to occur with inappropriate speed and very wide or badly worn tyres.
One of the best solutions to avoid aquaplaning is to reduce the speed in the first instance, so that the tyres can displace the water and the wheels can retain contact with the road surface.
(Página 228 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
8 Headlights - Low beam / dipped beam / short range  
   
8.2 Use of the low beam headlights
All motor vehicles and mopeds must use the low beam headlights (together with the position lights) when travelling:
Any hour of the day, when driving:
- On any lane of a road in which an additional circumstantial lane has been enabled.
- In a lane that has been enabled in a contrary direction to normal, that is, the use is exclusively reserved for certain users or due to exceptional circumstances, the direction for use has been changed.
- On the lane for the normal driving direction, adjacent to the one enabled for driving in the opposite direction than normal.
- In a reversible lane.
(Página 101 del manual 'Learning to drive')
